newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai pension cover tops 90 percent of firms.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai pension cover tops 90 percent of firms.

text.p: Shanghai's worker pension scheme now covers more than 90 percent of firms and should provide enough funds to see the city over a demographic "age hump" caused by the one-child policy, officials said on Thursday.

Shanghai is at the forefront of one of the most basic reforms of China's state-dominated financial system -- creating a system by which staff and workers can be guaranteed income to meet their basic needs after retirement.

It is also one of the building blocks of a social security system which needs to be in place before serious progress can be made on closing down the thousands of loss-making state enterprises around the country, analysts say.

A senior official from the Shanghai Pension Bureau, Zhu Zhichao, said the city's pension fund was set up in 1994 and was now taking in four percent of the wages of more than 4.2 million workers in the city.
This percentage contribution would rise by one percentage point a year until the year 2000 when it hits eight percent, he said.
"The basic framework is in place now, more than 90 percent of all enterprises and companies in the city have now joined the scheme," Zhu said.

In addition, all companies are required to contribute 25.5 percent of their total wage bill to the Pension Bureau, which uses the money to pay pensions to the 1.85 million retired workers in the city who receive a pension.
The individual contributions are being put in the pension fund to cover future requirements, he said, but declined to say how big the fund was.

With average salaries in Shanghai around 780 yuan ($94) a month, according to official statistics, a pension deduction of four percent from the salaries of the 4.2 million workers in the scheme would amount to more than 1.5 billion yuan per year.
But Zhu said this number was far in excess of the amount they actually take in due to a cut-off point for contributions for people with high salaries.
He said the Shanghai pension fund is managed by the state-run Pudong Development Bank which gives the Pension Bureau a guaranteed return of two percentage points above standard bank interest rates.
"For us, that means no risk," Zhu said. "They take the risk and have to pay us the extra two percent regardless of how they do."
An official from the Pudong Development Bank declined to give details of the size of Shanghai's pension fund or the rate at which is it growing.
But she said the money was mostly invested in treasury bills with a small portion invested in selected state-owned enterprises.
Zhu said the main challenge the pension fund needs to prepare for is a demographic "age hump" between the years 2020 and 2030.
China's one-child policy means the working population will gradually fall relative to the number of retiring staff workers, born in an age of unrestricted family size.
Asked if a return on the fund of two percentage points above bank deposit rates would be enough to handle the extra pension burden in those years, Zhu said:
"Our calculations indicate that the fund will allow us to handle the hump."
He said that, anyway, pension funds were forbidden from investing in higher-return but also higher-risk investments such as the stock market.
(US$1 = 8.3 yuan)
